description: In **100 days**, between April and July **1994**, hundreds of thousands of Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed in Rwanda. The fastest genocide of the century unfolded in full view of the world.

hero.hook: One hundred days. Hundreds of thousands dead. And a world that chose not to act.

blocks.text: Between April and July **1994**, in just **100 days**, Rwanda lived through a tragedy of rare intensity. Between **500,000** and **800,000** Tutsis, along with moderate Hutus, were murdered in a systematic campaign.
This genocide stands out for its speed and for the inaction of the international community. To understand 1994 is to understand colonial roots, political planning, and diplomatic silence.

In Rwanda, Hutus (about **85%**) and Tutsis (about **14%**) were not fixed “races” before colonization. The difference was mostly social and economic: a Hutu who grew rich in cattle could become a Tutsi, and the other way around.

In **1933**, the Belgian administration froze that identity on an **ethnic identity card**. People were sometimes sorted by the shape of the nose, or by the number of cows: past ten, you were a Tutsi.

Belgian settlers, shaped by racial theories, first relied on the Tutsis, then turned to the Hutu majority as independence approached in **1962**. Pogroms drove thousands of Tutsis into exile. Hatred became an inheritance.

sections.title: When identity becomes an ID card

blocks.text: In the 1990s, President **Juvénal Habyarimana** ran the country. His government was at war with the [[Rwandan Patriotic Front]], made up of Tutsi exiles. Extremists of [[Hutu Power]] trained the Interahamwe militias. [[Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines]] poured out hatred day after day and stripped Tutsis of their humanity.

blocks.caption: Rwanda in 1994, the scene of a planned genocide

blocks.text: On **April 6, 1994**, the presidential plane was shot down. Within the hour, roadblocks went up. About **8,000** people were killed every day. The killing was close-up work: neighbors, colleagues, local officials. This was not a spontaneous explosion. It was an organized operation.

On the ground, [[UNAMIR and General Dallaire]], the UN mission commanded by the Canadian Roméo Dallaire, had only a mandate to observe. Scarred by the failure in [[Somalia]], the United States held back any intervention. Even the word “genocide” was avoided, because under the 1948 Convention it would have forced governments to act.

blocks.caption: Paul Kagame and the RPF, whose offensive ended the massacres

blocks.text: France launched Operation [[Turquoise]] late in the day, officially humanitarian but criticized for easing the flight of the killers into [[Zaire]], today the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It was not the UN that stopped the killing. It was the RPF offensive, led by **Paul Kagame**, which took the capital, Kigali, on **July 4, 1994**.

After July 1994, the country had to judge the unjudgeable. The [[Gacaca]] courts, neighborhood tribunals, worked through nearly two million cases. The [[International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda]] tried the men who planned the killing. The Kigali memorial holds the remains of more than **250,000** victims.
